title: Hiring Manager: Roles, Responsibilities and How to Work with One (October 2026)
summary: Hiring managers own the final hiring decision. Learn their responsibilities and how they work with recruiters and HR. October 2026.
body_markdown:
Most people don’t think about[what is the hiring manager](https://www.dover.com/) ’s role until they’re already in the middle of an interview process, trying to read the room. Understanding what is the hiring manager and what they actually own makes every stage of the process clearer to work through, because the job starts long before you ever get a call.


**TLDR:**


-


A hiring manager owns the open role and makes the final call on who gets hired, not HR or recruiting.


-


Recruiters handle sourcing and logistics; hiring managers define requirements and lead substantive assessment.


-


HR sets the salary band; the hiring manager decides where within it a specific candidate should land.


-


Many stalled searches trace back to misalignment between hiring manager and recruiter instead of a shortage of candidates.


-


Some tools pair a free ATS with on-demand recruiting support, with an average cost per hire of around $4,800 and no long-term contract.


## What Is a Hiring Manager?


A hiring manager is the person who owns the open role, typically the direct supervisor the new hire will report to. When a position opens up, it is usually the hiring manager who kicks off the process by defining what the team needs, not HR.


The title can confuse people. Hiring managers typically do not work in HR or recruiting. They are functional leaders: department heads, engineering managers, VPs of Sales, or founders, and running a team is their primary job. Because they are accountable for the new hire’s performance once that person starts, they tend to have the final say on who gets an offer.


## Core Responsibilities of a Hiring Manager


A hiring manager’s involvement starts before the job is posted and extends past the final interview.


-


Define the role: what the team actually needs, required skills, level of seniority, and what “great” looks like


-


Write or review the[job description](https://www.dover.com/blog/job-description-guide) before it goes live


-


Partner with recruiting or HR to set the hiring timeline and process


-


Screen resumes or review shortlists from a recruiter


-


Conduct interviews, often including the first and final rounds


-


Assemble and coordinate the interview panel from within the team, building a[collaborative hiring process](https://www.dover.com/blog/why-a-collaborative-hiring-process-is-essential-for-startups) that matters more than most managers expect


-


Debrief with interviewers and synthesize feedback


-


Make the final candidate decision or provide the decisive recommendation to HR


-


Approve the offer terms and, in many cases, extend the offer directly


## Hiring Manager vs. Recruiter


Recruiters find and move candidates through the process; hiring managers decide who gets hired. Understanding[what type of recruiter is best](https://www.dover.com/blog/what-type-of-recruiter-is-best) for your situation shapes how well this division actually works.

Writes job description Reviews and approves Often drafts


Sourcing candidates Not involved ✓ Owns this

## Hiring Manager vs. HR


HR and the hiring manager both touch every hire, but they own different parts of it. HR handles compliance, compensation bands, benefits, and onboarding paperwork, while the hiring manager owns the business decision: which skills the team needs and whether a candidate can do the job.


These roles overlap at the offer stage and onboarding. HR confirms a proposed salary fits the approved band and that the offer letter meets legal requirements, while the hiring manager drives who gets the offer and focuses on integrating the new hire once they accept.


## Is the Hiring Manager Your Boss?


In most cases, yes. The hiring manager is typically the person you will report to once you start, which is exactly why they have final say over who gets hired.


The questions you ask should reflect that reality too. Asking the hiring manager what the team is struggling with, or what success looks like in the first six months, signals that you understand the relationship you are walking into.


## Hiring Manager Salary


“Hiring manager” is a role, not an occupation the BLS tracks on its own, so pay depends on the function that person leads. The closest proxy, the[U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reports](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/management/human-resources-managers.htm) , put the median annual wage for Human Resources Managers at approximately $149,000 in May 2025, while[management occupations broadly](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/management/) carried a median annual wage of $126,520 in May 2025. Industry, company size, and seniority level shift those figures considerably.


## How Hiring Managers and Recruiters Work Together


The partnership works best when the hiring manager treats the recruiter as a strategic partner, not an occasional check-in.


It starts with the intake meeting. A recruiter going into sourcing without a clear brief will build the wrong pipeline. A useful intake covers actual requirements versus nice-to-haves, what has failed in past searches, where strong candidates tend to come from, and what the interview process looks like end to end. Thirty minutes here saves weeks later.


From there, the recruiter owns sourcing and initial screening. What they need from the hiring manager is fast, specific feedback on the first candidate batch: not “these aren’t quite right,” but “this person has the systems experience we need; this one is too junior at the infrastructure layer.” That signal lets a recruiter recalibrate before burning through the candidate pool.


## What Makes a Hiring Manager Effective


Structured process separates hiring managers who consistently build strong teams from those who spend months re-opening the same roles.


The most concrete differentiator is how a hiring manager handles evaluation before interviews begin. Writing a clear rubric (or an[interview scorecard](https://www.dover.com/blog/interview-scorecard-guide) ) forces explicit thinking about what “strong” actually means for each competency. Without it, panel debrief turns into a negotiation between gut reactions instead of an analysis of evidence.


A few behaviors that show up consistently in managers who hire well:


-


They conduct[structured interviews for startups](https://www.dover.com/blog/how-to-interview-candidates-for-your-startup) , asking the same core questions of every candidate so comparisons are genuinely apples-to-apples


-


They give recruiters specific, calibrated feedback within 24-48 hours of each screen instead of batching it at the end


-


They separate “would I enjoy working with this person” from “can this person do the work” to avoid affinity bias driving decisions


-


They define the role’s first 90-day success criteria before the search opens, not after an offer falls through


## Common Challenges Hiring Managers Face


The most common breakdowns:


-


Job descriptions that reflect what the team had, not what it actually needs next. For teams without a full-time recruiter, understanding[what a fractional recruiter is](https://www.dover.com/blog/what-is-a-fractional-recruiter-guide) can open a practical middle path. Writing from memory of the last person in the role anchors the search to the past and filters out candidates who might be a stronger fit for where the team is heading.


-


Time. Reviewing resumes, running interviews, and coordinating a panel does not pause when the quarter gets hard. Searches stall because the hiring manager is the bottleneck, not because candidates are scarce.


-


Objectivity drift over a long search. After months of interviews, the bar moves without anyone noticing. Candidates interviewed late in the process get measured against exhaustion, not the original rubric.


-


Stakeholder misalignment mid-search. A recruiter sources to one brief; the panel interviews to another; the hiring manager makes a call that surprises HR at the offer stage.


## The Hiring Manager’s Role in Salary and Offer Decisions


HR sets the band; the hiring manager decides where within it to land.


In most organizations, a compensation team or HR sets salary ranges before a search opens. The hiring manager then advocates for where a specific candidate should fall inside that band, and typically has more discretion over adjacent variables: equity, title level, start date, sign-on. A hiring manager who understands the budget and the candidate’s alternatives will use those levers strategically.


That discretion carries real stakes.[SHRM’s 2025 benchmarking data](https://www.shrm.org/about/press-room/shrm-releases-2025-benchmarking-reports--how-does-your-organizat) puts the average cost per hire for non-executive roles at $5,475. Lowballing a strong candidate to stay comfortable in the band can mean restarting a search that costs more than the salary difference would have.


## What Is the Hiring Manager’s Role at Lean Startups? How Dover Helps Handle the Full Load


Many hiring managers at early-stage startups absorb both sides of the hiring equation: defining the role, running interviews, and managing the pipeline without a dedicated internal recruiter to split the load. The practical question is where to draw the line between what a tool can handle and when a person needs to be involved.


For inbound-heavy roles where the challenge is managing applicant volume, structuring interviews, and keeping candidates moving, an ATS handles the infrastructure: distributing job posts across 50+ boards, automating scheduling, tracking applicants through each stage. Some free ATS tools are built specifically for this layer, including a no-code careers page. Dover’s[free ATS for startups](https://www.dover.com/ats) covers this, with AI applicant scoring on the $199/month Premium plan, and no engineering support required.


Where an ATS reaches its structural limit is active sourcing: finding candidates who are not applying, running outreach campaigns, and building a pipeline for a senior or specialized role where inbound volume alone won’t close the search. That’s where layering in a fractional recruiter tends to change the outcome. On-demand[fractional recruiting](https://www.dover.com/blog/fractional-recruiting-guide) services connect hiring managers with experienced recruiters who work as dedicated partners on specific roles, handling the active sourcing an ATS can’t. Dover’s recruiter marketplace operates this way, with an average cost per hire of about $4,800 across roles (actual costs vary by seniority and hiring complexity), no long-term contract; and when both the ATS and the recruiter operate in the same shared system, the hiring manager avoids the coordination overhead of managing two separate pipelines.


## FAQs


### What is the difference between a hiring manager and a recruiter?


A hiring manager owns the open role and makes the final call on who gets hired; a recruiter handles the practical work of finding and moving candidates through the process. In practice, the hiring manager defines what the role actually requires and leads substantive interviews, while the recruiter manages sourcing, screening, scheduling, and offer logistics. The partnership breaks down when the hiring manager provides a vague brief or goes dark between stages, which is why alignment at the intake meeting matters more than most people expect.


### What’s the best way for a hiring manager to work with a recruiter without slowing down the search?


The single highest-impact move is a thorough intake meeting before sourcing begins: cover actual requirements versus nice-to-haves, what has failed in past searches, and what the interview process looks like end to end. From there, giving the recruiter fast, specific feedback on the first candidate batch, detailed enough to recalibrate sourcing before the candidate pool is exhausted, prevents most of the delays that stall searches. A weekly sync cadence and early recruiter involvement in offer conversations tend to close the coordination gaps where strong candidates drop off.


### Do I need a recruiter if I’m already using an ATS?


An ATS and a recruiter solve different problems. An ATS structures your pipeline, distributes job posts, automates scheduling, and tracks candidates, but it doesn’t source people who aren’t applying or bring market knowledge about where strong candidates in a given function tend to be found. For inbound-heavy roles, an ATS often handles the load. For senior or competitive roles that depend on active outreach, a fractional recruiter adds the sourcing layer the ATS can’t provide.


## Final Thoughts on How Hiring Managers, Recruiters, and HR Work Together


When the lines between hiring manager, recruiter, and HR are clear, searches move faster and the right candidates get offers. When those lines blur, even a strong candidate pool does not save you. Knowing[what is the hiring manager](https://www.dover.com/) ’s role in all of this is the starting point: they own the business decision, not the process plumbing. The most common structural fix for lean teams absorbing all three functions is separating the process layer from the sourcing layer, using an ATS to manage pipeline infrastructure, and adding a fractional recruiter on top when a role needs active outreach. Whether those two layers live in separate systems or a single shared one tends to determine how much coordination overhead the hiring manager ends up carrying.
